human_tolerance.notes: Extremely curious and will often attempt to enter buildings, moving anything they can and gnawing woodwork; once inside a house or cabin they can be very destructive, tearing out insulation and mattress stuffing for nesting material. Occupies a wide variety of forest habitat and is expanding its range into hardwood forests.

phases.name: mating
phases.note: Squirrels are solitary but pair for mating in February and March, females entering estrus for only one day. Males must temporarily leave their territories to find a reproductive female, producing a scramble competition mating system in which females may mate with 4 to 16 males. Gestation is 31 to 35 days.

phases.name: young
phases.note: Litters of typically three or four (range one to five) are born in spring; offspring are pink and hairless at birth weighing about 10 g, grow at roughly 1.8 g per day while nursing, first emerge from the natal nest at around 42 days, continue nursing to about 70 days, and reach adult body size at 125 days.

phases.name: caching
phases.note: White spruce cones mature in late July and are harvested by red squirrels in August and September, stored in a central cache or midden that supplies energy and nutrients for survival over the winter and for reproduction the following spring. White spruce has two- to six-year masting cycles, so a squirrel is likely to experience both very high and very low food levels in its lifetime.

vocalizations.description: A high-frequency alarm call given when an avian predator has been detected.
A low, barking call given when a ground predator has been detected; either the high-frequency aerial call or this bark may be produced, or the two mixed, as a predator approaches.

The species' noisy chatter and rattling, the everyday vocalisation of an animal that makes itself conspicuous with its lively habits; not a single stereotyped call but a continuous range of territorial and contact chatter.

taxonomy.note: GBIF backbone gives family Sciuridae and authority (Erxleben, 1777); ITIS scientific-name search returns TSN 180166 with the same authority. The southwestern red squirrel T. fremonti was long conspecific and a 2016 phylogenetic study found it a distinct species, so it is excluded here.

external.note: GBIF usageKey 2437282 from species/match; ITIS TSN 180166 from the ITIS scientific-name search; NCBI taxon id 10009 and IUCN category least concern (Q211005) from Wikidata P685 and P141.

common_names.note: English label from Wikidata Q326976. No French or German vernacular is recorded on that item, so none is written here rather than borrowing the Eurasian red squirrel's names, which would be wrong: 'American red squirrels should not be confused with Eurasian red squirrels (Sciurus vulgaris); since the ranges of these species do not overlap, they are both commonly referred to as simply "red squirrel"'.

conservation.note: Wikidata P141 = least concern (Q211005); 'American red squirrels are abundant and not of conservation concern throughout much of their range.'

range.note: 'Their range includes: most of Canada, excluding northern areas with no tree cover and the southwestern coast of British Columbia; the southern half of Alaska; the Rocky Mountains area of the United States, and northern half of the eastern United States.' The introduced population is on Newfoundland, which is part of Canada, so it is recorded in both lists.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: 'Red squirrels are agile climbers' from ADF&G; on the ground they move and forage at cone middens, stumps and rocks. Both gaits are Walk; there is no powered flight and no separate bound described.

traits.nest_type.note: Authored, and the choice is not clean: 'Nests are most commonly constructed of grass in the branches of trees. Nests are also excavated from witches' broom ... or cavities in the trunks of spruce, poplar, and walnut trees.' The most common nest is a grass dome in a branch, which the schema has no exact term for; Cavity is recorded because the source states cavity nesting outright and because cavity is the winter shelter tag, and the branch nest is carried as a nest_platform resource. A reviewer may reasonably prefer Cup here.

traits.perching.note: Not a perching animal in the passerine sense: it climbs, leaps and rests on branches, but the schema's perching flag is set to false, as for the eastern gray squirrel record in this kit.

traits.senses.note: hearing High from the predator-class-specific alarm calls, which are described as difficult to localize because of their short, low-amplitude, high-frequency character, implying fine auditory discrimination. vision_color authored from the reddish coat and the white belly the species is identified by. olfaction set to Med with no sourced claim found; scent-marking is documented for deer in this kit but not for this squirrel, so nothing stronger is claimed.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg (0.2007 kg falls in the Small band, under 1 kg).

traits.mass_kg.note: Mean of EltonTraits MamFuncDat BodyMass-Value 201.17 g and PanTHERIA AdultBodyMass_g 200.24 g, giving 0.2007 kg, consistent with the source's 'small, 200-250 g' squirrel.

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of 28-35 cm 'total length (including tail)', consistent with PanTHERIA AdultHeadBodyLen 188.42 mm plus a bushy tail.

traits.lifespan_y.note: 'Females that survive to one year of age have a life expectancy of 3.5 years and a maximum lifespan of 8 years.' The conditional expectation is used because it is the only typical-longevity figure the source gives; the same section notes 'American red squirrels experience severe early mortality (on average only 22% survive to one year of age)'.

traits.home_range_ha.note: Derived from a sourced figure rather than invented: 'Offspring that do not receive a midden from their mother typically settle within 150 m (3 territory diameters) of their natal territory', so a territory diameter is about 50 m and a circular territory of that diameter is about 0.2 ha. The source states no home range in hectares, so this is a conversion of a settlement distance, and the circular-territory assumption is a judgement.

traits.diet.note: EltonTraits Diet-Vend 20 and Diet-Vunk 10 both map to vertebrate (30), Diet-Fruit 20 to fruit, Diet-Nect 10 to nectar, Diet-Seed 20 to seed, and Diet-PlantO 20 to browse for buds, needles, leaves and mushrooms. The vertebrate share matches the source's 'animal material such as bird eggs or even snowshoe hare leverets (young)'. Note that the sourced seed share understates this species locally: 'In the Yukon, extensive behavioral observations suggest white spruce seeds (Picea glauca) comprise more than 50% of a red squirrel's diet'. The dataset's range-wide average is used here and the local dominance is recorded in this note rather than silently substituted.

traits.social.note: 'Red squirrels are highly territorial and asocial with very few non-reproductive physical interactions (0.6% of all recorded behaviours in one 19-year study)'; ADF&G adds 'Red squirrels are solitary but pair for mating in February and March.' Solitary with a group size of 1 is the accurate encoding; the mating pair is seasonal and does not make the species a pair-forming one.

traits.activity_pattern.note: The source calls it a 'diurnal mammal' and ADF&G adds 'Red squirrels are primarily diurnal, but have been occasionally observed exhibiting nocturnal behavior, collecting food on moonlit nights', so the occasional night foraging is not treated as a second activity pattern.

traits.defense.note: Mob: 'The non-reproductive physical interactions recorded were all instances of chasing an intruder from a territory', and ADF&G notes the animal is 'extremely curious' and will enter buildings. Aggressive pursuit of an intruder is a territorial-mob response, which fits the schema's Mob better than Flee for a squirrel that never yields ground.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement from ADF&G's 'being extremely curious, will often attempt to enter buildings': the animal approaches people and buildings rather than avoiding them, but it defends a territory aggressively against conspecifics, so a middling value is used rather than a very low one.

habitat.use.note: EltonTraits ForStrat-Value 'Ar' gives the primary stratum as arboreal. The ground share of 0.2 is authored judgement for the ground-level foraging described in the sources, where cone cuttings collect on stumps and rocks and where middens sit on the ground.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Authored: the species keeps several nests within its territory and moves them between nests, and nests are excavated in trunk cavities of spruce, poplar and walnut, so cavity; the source describes nest construction directly but not a single resting-shelter tag.

habitat.resources.note: Food weights follow traits.diet, with the two EltonTraits vertebrate codes split into invertebrate 0.1 and small_vertebrate 0.2 to keep the predation resources separable for the importer; the source's animal food is bird eggs and snowshoe hare leverets, which spans both. Nesting weight is split 0.6 cavity / 0.4 nest_platform to reflect the two nest types described, with the weighting a judgement that follows 'most commonly constructed of grass in the branches' for the branch nest but keeps the cavity nest substantial because the source states it outright.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: ADF&G: 'Red squirrels are agile climbers and, being extremely curious, will often attempt to enter buildings, upsetting anything they can move and gnawing on woodwork. Once in a house or cabin, they can be very destructive, tearing out insulation and mattress stuffing for use as nesting material.' Exploiter follows from that behaviour, which is thriving on human structures rather than merely tolerating them.

seasonal.strategy.note: 'defends a year-round exclusive territory' and there is no migration or dormancy in the source; a squirrel that must survive winter on its own midden cache is active all year.

seasonal.phases.note: Mating window from ADF&G ('pair for mating in February and March') and Wikipedia's one-day estrus with 31-35 days' gestation; the young window from the birth, growth and weaning figures in the Reproduction section; the caching window from 'White spruce cones mature in late July and are harvested by red squirrels in August and September' with the cache intended 'for survival over the winter and reproduction the following spring'.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Juvenile duration from 'reach adult body size at 125 days', with first emergence from the nest at around 42 days and nursing to about 70 days; 'Females can breed for the first time at one year of age' supports the adult stage. Scale is authored judgement, informed by the newborn weight of about 10 g against the 200.7 g adult.

vocalizations.alarm_aerial.note: ADF&G: 'Red squirrels produce high frequency alarm calls when avian predators have been detected.' The call_id is authored, and the state it is assigned to - aerial predator - is the schema's Alarm context.

vocalizations.bark.note: ADF&G: 'and low, barking calls for ground predators, although either call may be produced or mixed when a predator approaches.' The call_id is authored from the word 'barking' in the source.

vocalizations.chatter.note: ADF&G: the squirrel 'makes itself quite conspicuous with its lively habits and noisy chatter'. The source does not describe the chatter as a distinct stereotyped call, so the description says so rather than inventing a rendering; the call_id is authored.

vocalizations.note: All three entries rest on the Alaska Department of Fish and Game species profile, chosen because the Wikipedia article carries no vocalization section at all and this profile is a United States state government source, hence public domain. Time windows and cooldowns are authored judgement, since no open source quantifies them, and no frequency bands are given so freq_hz is omitted.

look.note: Colours from the two sources: 'reddish fur with a white venter (underbelly)' (Wikipedia) and ADF&G's 'rusty red above, with a whitish belly, gray sides, and ears that are tufted in winter', 'In summer, a dark stripe on the side separates the upper rusty color from the white of the belly', and 'The bushy tail is often a lighter orange or red with light tipped hairs'. The snout is coloured from the belly slot and the ears from the markings slot for the grey sides and winter tufts; an enlarged tail part renders the characteristic bushy tail. Proportions are authored judgement for a small, compact, short-legged tree squirrel with a tail about as long as the body.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared ground-forager program. food_tag set to seed, the item the sources name as the staple. flee_m 10 m and calm_m 20 m are small, because this is a 200 g animal defending a fixed territory rather than a wide-ranging one, and a squirrel that has never yielded ground to an intruder is not a creature that flees far. flee_gait and forage_gait both walk, since the animal is described as an agile climber rather than a runner. rest_sun_lo_deg -90 and rest_sun_hi_deg -6 follow the program's own prescription for a diurnal species, which the sources confirm.
